# Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedback applied to Speech Zone Detection

This project has received funding from the SOUNDS European Training
Network, an European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation
programme under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie grant agreement No. 956369.

###### Abstract

Modern cars provide versatile tools to enhance speech communication.
While an in-car communication (ICC) system aims at enhancing
communication between the passengers by playing back desired speech via
loudspeakers in the car, these loudspeaker signals may disturb a speech
enhancement system required for hands-free telephony and automatic
speech recognition. In this paper, we focus on speech zone detection,
i.e. detecting which passenger in the car is speaking, which is a
crucial component of the speech enhancement system. We propose a
model-based feedback estimation method to improve robustness of speech
zone detection against ICC feedback. Specifically, since the zone
detection system typically does not have access to the ICC loudspeaker
signals, the proposed method estimates the feedback signal from the
observed microphone signals based on a free-field propagation model
between the loudspeakers and the microphones as well as the ICC gain. We
propose an efficient recursive implementation in the short-time Fourier
transform domain using convolutive transfer functions. A realistic
simulation study indicates that the proposed method allows to increase
the ICC gain by about $`6`$ dB while still achieving robust speech zone
detection results.

speaker activity detection, speech zone detection

## 1 Introduction

While multiple built-in loudspeakers for passenger entertainment in cars
have been a standard for decades, modern car cabins are increasingly
equipped with multiple distributed microphones for applications such as
hands-free telephony, automatic speech recognition or in-car
communication (ICC). The former applications are designed for
communication with external parties and require speech enhancement, e.g.
beamforming or noise reduction \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2),
[3](#bib.bib3)\]. On the other hand, ICC systems are designed to enhance
speech intelligibility between passengers by reinforcing desired speech
signals in the car cabin \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5),
[6](#bib.bib6)\]. Often, this is achieved by recording the speech signal
of a front passenger and reproducing it over loudspeakers at the rear
cabin (see
[Fig. 1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
to prevent the driver from turning around or shouting in order to be
understood. The main challenge of ICC systems is to stabilize the closed
electroacoustic loop resulting from the feedback of the loudspeaker
signals to the microphones \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5),
[6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9),
[10](#bib.bib10)\]. In practice, hands-free and ICC systems often run on
different processors with highly restricted information exchange meaning
that the loudspeaker signals used for the ICC system are generally not
available for the hands-free system, which rules out a joint processing
of both systems as proposed in \[[11](#bib.bib11)\].

Depending on the ICC gain, the speech enhancement performance of the
hands-free system may be substantially degraded by the ICC system. In
this paper, we specifically focus on its influence on speech zone
detection: When speech zones are defined in the car (one zone for each
seat) to achieve speech enhancement for each zone individually, it is
required to distinguish which zone is active, i.e. which passenger is
speaking. According to \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], speech zone detection can
be achieved by evaluating the maximum signal power ratios of
passenger-dedicated microphones, as the speaker-dedicated microphone
typically shows the highest signal power. However, this assumption may
be violated in combination with an ICC system since the signal power of
microphones close to ICC loudspeakers may exceed that of the
speaker-dedicated microphone. One might consider classical feedback
cancellation techniques \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] to remove the ICC feedback
from the microphone signals. This would however require a loudspeaker
reference signal, which in practice is not available for speech zone
detection.

In this paper, a model-based feedback signal estimation method is
proposed. This method estimates the ICC feedback contribution in the
observed microphone signals without requiring access to the clean
loudspeaker signals and by only considering free-field propagation
between the loudspeakers and microphones. We propose an efficient
recursive implementation in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT)
domain using convolutive transfer functions (CTF) \[[13](#bib.bib13)\].
Finally, we suppress the ICC feedback contribution from the power
spectral densities (PSD) of the observed microphone signals, which helps
to improve robustness of speech zone detection against ICC feedback.

Fig. 1: Exemplary car setup with independent hands-free and in-car
communication (ICC) systems. Dashed circles symbolize speech zones.

## 2 Signal Model

We consider a car environment with a single speaker, $`M`$
passenger-dedicated microphones and an ICC system with $`L`$
loudspeakers (see
[Fig. 2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")).
The observed microphone signals $`y_{m}(n)`$, with the microphone index
$`m\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\{0,...,M{-}1\}`$ and the sample time
index $`n`$, consist of three components: The direct signals
$`y_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(n)`$, i.e. the microphone signals due to in-car
speech (including reverberation), the ICC feedback signals
$`y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(n)`$ induced by the ICC loudspeakers as well as
noise $`v_{m}(n)`$, i.e.

|     |                            |                                                                            |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle y_{m}(n)`$ | $`\displaystyle=y_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(n)+y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(n)+v_{m}(n)\,.`$ |     | (1) |

This paper will only consider the low-noise case, where $`v_{m}(n)`$ can
be neglected. The desired direct signal $`y_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(n)`$ is the
dry speech signal $`s(n)`$ filtered with the acoustic impulse response
$`h_{\mathrm{d},{m}}(n)`$ from the speech source to the $`m`$-th
microphone. Likewise, the feedback signal $`y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(n)`$ can
be expressed as

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\!y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(n)=u(n)\ast h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)\;\text{with }h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\textstyle\sum_{i=0}^{L-\hskip-0.5pt1}h_{i,m}(n),`$ |     | (2) |

where $`u(n)`$ denotes the ICC loudspeaker signal (same for all
loudspeakers), $`\{\ast\}`$ denotes convolution and $`h_{i,m}(n)`$ is
the acoustic impulse response from the $`i`$-th loudspeaker to the
$`m`$-th microphone. $`m\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$ refers to the ICC
reference microphone channel that is reinforced in the car cabin.

The ICC and speech enhancement system including the speech zone
detection are implemented in the STFT domain. Accordingly, the signal
model needs to be formulated in the same domain. Since the impulse
responses $`h_{\mathrm{d},{m}}(n)`$ and $`h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)`$ are
typically longer than the STFT frame size, and especially due to the
recursive ICC structure (see
[Fig. 2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")),
filtering in the STFT domain requires a multi-frame approach such as
crossband filtering \[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)\]. To reduce
computational complexity, we will consider the convolutive transfer
function (CTF) approximation \[[13](#bib.bib13)\], which only considers
band-to-band filters, i.e.

|     |                          |                                                                                                                         |     |
| --- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle Y(k,l)`$ | $`\displaystyle=S(k,l)\ast H(k,l)={\hskip-4.0pt\begin{array}[]{c}\scriptstyle{\mathclap{N\_{\hskip-0.5ptH}-1}}\\[0.0pt] |

{\text{{$\sum$}}}\\[-0.5pt]
\scriptstyle{\mathclap{l^{\prime}\!=0}}\end{array}\hskip-3.0pt}S(k,l{-}l^{\prime})\,H(k,l^{\prime})\,,`$ | |

where $`k`$ denotes the frequency index and $`l`$ the frame index,
$`S(k,l)`$ and $`Y(k,l)`$ are the STFT representations of the input and
output signal, respectively, and $`H(k,l)`$ is the CTF consisting of
$`N_{\hskip-0.5ptH}`$ filter coefficients (we only consider causal
coefficients). Here, $`\{\ast\}`$ denotes the convolution over frames.

In this work, we model the ICC system (see
[Fig. 2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
using a linear model, where it should be realized that this is an
approximation of a real ICC system, such as e.g. \[[4](#bib.bib4),
[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6)\]. The forward path incorporates the
static ICC CTF $`H_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}(k,l)`$, which models the known ICC
processing delay $`\tau_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}`$, as well as a dynamic,
real-valued and frequency-dependent ICC gain $`\alpha(k,l)`$. Since
$`\tau_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}`$ is fixed, the ICC gain $`\alpha(k,l)`$ is the
only variable parameter that needs to be transmitted from the ICC to the
zone detection at runtime. However, the ICC gain is usually slowly
time-varying and thus requires no frame-wise transmission (the frame
index will be omitted below). $`G_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(k,l)`$ is a linear
model of the ICC feedback cancellation filter (see \[[5](#bib.bib5),
[6](#bib.bib6), [8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\] for
practical examples), which aims at subtracting the feedback signal from
the ICC input signal to stabilize the ICC system and only amplify the
desired direct signal.

For better readability, the frequency and frame indices $`k,l`$ are
omitted hereinafter in this section. Using this signal model, it can be
shown that the loudspeaker signal $`U`$ and the $`m`$-th feedback signal
$`Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}`$ are given by

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\displaystyle U=\alpha\,H_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\ast(Y_{0}-G_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\ast U)\,,
``` |  | (6) |
|  |
``` math
\displaystyle Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}=H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}\ast U\,.
``` |  | (7) |

By substituting
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
into
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")),
the feedback signal can be written as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\boxed{Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}=\alpha\,H_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\ast\big(H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}\ast Y_{0}-G_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\ast Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}\big).}`$ |  | (8) |

We consider only strictly causal CTFs (exclusively depending on past
frames) to ensure that the recursive filters in
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")),
([8](#S2.E8 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
and in the following equations are realizable.

To get a deeper understanding of the influence of the feedback
cancellation filter $`G_{L,0}`$, one can define a mismatch

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}`$ | $`\displaystyle=H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}-G_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}`$ |  | (9) |

between the acoustic transfer function $`H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}`$ and
$`G_{L,0}`$. Resolving
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
for $`G_{L,0}`$ and inserting into
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
yields

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} U&=\alpha\,H_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\ast\big(Y_{0}-H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\ast U+\Delta H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\ast U\big)\\
&=\alpha\,H_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\ast\big(Y_{0}-Y_{0}^{\mathrm{fb}}+\Delta H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\ast U\big).\end{aligned}`$ |  | (10) |

By using
$`Y_{0}\,\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\,Y_{0}^{\mathrm{d}}+Y_{0}^{\mathrm{fb}}`$
and substituting
([10](#S2.E10 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
into
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")),
the feedback signal can be written as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\boxed{Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}=\alpha\,H_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\ast\big(H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}\ast Y_{0}^{\mathrm{d}}+\Delta H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\ast Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}\big).}`$ |  | (11) |

According to this, the mismatch $`\Delta H_{L,0}`$ can be interpreted as
a measure of the amount of feedback reduction:
$`\Delta H_{L,0}\,\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\,0`$, i.e.
$`G_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\,\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\,H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}`$,
corresponds to perfect feedback cancellation (only the desired direct
signal $`Y_{0}^{\mathrm{d}}`$ would be amplified since there would be no
recursion in
([11](#S2.E11 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")));
$`\Delta H_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0ptH_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}`$,
i.e. $`G_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$, represents no
feedback cancellation.

## 3 Feedback Signal Estimation

In practice, the feedback signals have to be estimated based on the
observed microphone signals $`Y_{m}(k,l)`$ without knowledge of the
loudspeaker signal $`U(k,l)`$. For this purpose, a feedback signal
estimator can be derived from
([8](#S2.E8 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \hat{Y}_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(k,l)=\;&\,\alpha(k)\,\hat{H}_{\mathrm{f},{m}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)\ast{Y}_{0}(k,l)\;-\\
&\alpha_{\mathrm{r}}\hskip-0.5pt(k)\,\hat{H}_{\mathrm{r}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)\ast\hat{Y}_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(k,l)\,,\end{aligned}`$ |  | (12) |

where
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{f},{m}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)\,\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\,{H}_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)\hskip 0.5pt{\ast}\hskip 0.5pt\hat{H}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(k,l)`$
denotes the feed-forward CTF and
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{r}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)\,\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\,{H}_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)\ast\hat{G}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(k,l)`$
the recursive CTF of the feedback signal estimator, respectively (see
[Fig. 3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")),
and $`\{\hat{\cdot}\}`$ denotes estimated or modeled quantities. We
consider only strictly causal coefficients of the CTFs
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{f},{m}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)`$ and
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{r}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)`$. Furthermore, we introduced
$`\alpha_{\mathrm{r}}(k)`$ to ensure stability of the estimator,
as described below.

According to \[[14](#bib.bib14), [13](#bib.bib13)\], the CTFs
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{f},{m}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)`$ and
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{r}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)`$ can be computed from the
corresponding time-domain filters

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\!\!\hat{h}_{\mathrm{f},{m}}(n)=h_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}(n)\hskip 0.5pt{\ast}\hskip 0.5pt\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n),\;\hat{h}_{\mathrm{r}}(n)=h_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}(n)\hskip 0.5pt{\ast}\hskip 0.5pt\hat{g}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)\,.`$ |  | (13) |

The ICC transfer function $`h_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}(n)`$ incorporates the
known ICC processing delay $`\tau_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}`$. The acoustic
impulse response $`\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)`$ can be either measured
or modeled. In this work, we consider a simple free-field propagation
model. Accordingly, the acoustic impulse response from the $`i`$-th
loudspeaker to the $`m`$-th microphone are approximated by

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{h}_{i,m}(n)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\beta_{i,m}}{D_{i,m}}\,\delta(n\hskip 1.0pt{-}\hskip 1.0pt\tau_{i,m})\;\text{ with }\tau_{i,m}=\Big\lfloor\frac{{f_{s}\,\cdot\,D_{i,m}}}{{c}}\Big\rfloor,`$ |  | (14) |

where $`D_{i,m}`$ is the distance between the $`i`$-th loudspeaker and
$`m`$-th microphone, $`\beta_{i,m}`$ is a gain factor that incorporates
the individual sensitivity of the loudspeakers and microphones^(†)^(†)
$`\beta_{i,m}`$ reflects the level difference between the loudspeaker
and microphone signal that would be observed in a free field at
$`D_{i,m}\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt1`$m. It could also include the
directivity of loudspeakers and microphones which is not considered
here.. Relative to
([9](#S2.E9 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")),
we propose to model the time-domain feedback cancellation filter as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{g}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)=(1-\lambda)\,\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$ |  | (15) |

with $`\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$ as described above. The mismatch
factor $`\lambda\hskip 1.0pt{\in}\hskip 1.0pt[0,1]`$ introduced herein
is used to model the amount of feedback reduction, where higher values
of $`\lambda`$ correspond to less feedback cancellation when assuming
that $`\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)\approx h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$.

In practice, it is crucial to ensure stability of the recursive filter
in
([12](#S3.E12 "In 3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
at runtime, where it should be noted that stability of the ICC system
does not guarantee stability of the feedback signal estimator. For this
purpose, the gain $`\alpha_{\mathrm{r}}(k)`$ of the recursive CTF is
upper-limited

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\alpha_{\mathrm{r}}(k)=\min\big\{\alpha(k),\,\alpha_{\mathrm{r,max}}(k)-\delta\big\}\,,`$ |  | (16) |

where $`\alpha_{\mathrm{r,max}}(k)`$ characterizes the stability border
of the recursive filter in
([12](#S3.E12 "In 3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
and $`\delta`$ is a small positive value (we used
$`\delta\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0.2`$ in this work).
$`\alpha_{\mathrm{r,max}}(k)`$ can be determined as the maximum
positive, real-valued gain for each subband $`k`$, where all poles of
the recursive filter

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{H}_{k}(z)`$ | $`\displaystyle=1\,\big/\left(1+\textstyle\sum_{l=1}^{L_{\mathrm{H}}}\alpha_{\mathrm{r,max}}(k)\,\hat{H}_{\mathrm{r}}(k,l)\,z^{-l}\right)`$ |  | (17) |

are strictly within the unit circle \[[16](#bib.bib16)\].

## 4 Zone Detection Robust Against ICC Feedback

In this section, we describe an energy-based speech zone detection
approach and moreover propose a method to increase its robustness
against ICC feedback using the feedback signal estimates of
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection").

### 4.1 Energy-Based Speech Zone Detection

In \[[12](#bib.bib12)\], it was proposed to perform energy-based speech
speech zone detection based on the signal power ratios (SPR)^(†)^(†)
Originally, the authors used the SPR for speaker activity detection.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\operatorname{SPR}}_{m}(k,l)`$ | $`\displaystyle=10\,\log_{10}\frac{\max\big\{\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}(k,l),\epsilon\big\}}{\max\Bigg\{\displaystyle\max_{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle m^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}}}{{\scriptscriptstyle m^{\prime}\neq m}}}\big\{\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!,m^{\prime}}(k,l)\big\},\epsilon\Bigg\}}`$ |  | (18) |

of passenger-dedicated microphones, where
$`\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}(k,l)`$ is the estimated
PSD of the $`m`$-th microphone signal, $`\mathcal{M}`$ is the set of all
microphones and $`\epsilon`$ is a small positive number. A broadband SPR
value can be determined by averaging over a set of frequencies
$`k\hskip 1.0pt{\in}\hskip 1.0pt\mathcal{K_{\text{speech}}}`$ assumed to
contain speech energy (we used $`100`$ Hz … $`8`$ kHz), i.e.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\overline{\operatorname{SPR}}_{m}(l)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{\text{speech}}|}\hskip 9.24994pt\,{\hskip-4.0pt\begin{array}[]{c}\scriptstyle{\mathclap{}}\\[-2.0pt]
{\text{{$\sum$}}}\\[-2.0pt]
\scriptstyle{\mathclap{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\text{speech}}}}\end{array}\hskip-3.0pt}\operatorname{SPR}_{m}(k,l)\,.`$ |  |

The active zone is finally identified as the passenger-dedicated (=
zone-dedicated) microphone with the largest broadband SPR, i.e.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\zeta_{\text{active}}(l)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\arg\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\,\overline{\operatorname{SPR}}_{m}(l)\,,`$ |  | (22) |

where $`\zeta\hskip 1.0pt{\in}\hskip 1.0pt\mathcal{M}`$ are the possible
speech zones.

Robustness of this speech zone detection approach against ICC feedback
could be increased by using direct signal PSD estimates
$`\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}^{\mathrm{d}}(k,l)`$ (no
contribution of ICC feedback) instead of the microphone signal PSDs
$`\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}(k,l)`$ to compute the
SPR in
([18](#S4.E18 "In 4.1 Energy-Based Speech Zone Detection ‣ 4 Zone Detection Robust Against ICC Feedback ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")).
Hereinafter, we propose an estimation of the direct signal PSDs using
the feedback signal estimates from
[Section 3](#S3 "3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection").

### 4.2 Estimation of the Direct Signal PSD

One could consider directly subtracting the estimated feedback signal
$`\hat{Y}_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(k,l)`$ from the observed microphone signal
$`Y_{m}(k,l)`$ to obtain a direct signal estimate
$`\hat{Y}_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(k,l)`$ in a first step. However, this
approach is highly sensitive to estimation errors such as phase errors.
Therefore we propose to estimate the direct signal PSD in the power
domain, which enables a better control of estimation errors. The
microphone signal PSD $`\Phi_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}(k,l)`$
is defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \!\E\hskip-0.5pt\big\{|Y_{m}(k,l)|^{2}\big\}=\,&\E\hskip-0.5pt\big\{|Y_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(k,l)|^{2}\big\}+\E\big\{|Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(k,l)|^{2}\big\}\,+\\
&\,2\,\Re\big\{\hskip-0.5pt\E\hskip-0.5pt\big\{Y_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(k,l)\,Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}*}(k,l)\big\}\!\big\}\,,\end{aligned}`$ |  | (23) |

where $`\E\{\cdot\}`$ denotes the expectation operator and
$`\Re\{\cdot\}`$ the real value operator. It can be shown that the cross
term
$`\E\big\{Y_{m}^{\mathrm{d}}(k,l)\,Y_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}*}(k,l)\big\}`$ is
negligible if the STFT frame size
$`N\hskip 1.0pt{<}\hskip 1.0pt\tau_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\hskip 1.0pt{+}\hskip 1.0pt\min_{i}\{\tau_{i,m}\}`$
(see ([14](#S3.E14 "In 3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")))
and the source signal $`S(k,l)`$ is a zero-mean random signal. Moreover,
this condition implicitly entails that the CTFs
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{r}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)`$ and
$`\hat{H}_{\mathrm{f\hskip-0.5pt},{m}}\hskip-0.5pt(k,l)`$ in
([12](#S3.E12 "In 3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
are strictly causal, which ensures the realizability of the feedback
signal estimator.

​​​Real-life scenarios in the car do not fully comply with the conditions
stated above as speech signals are short-time stationary and
reverberation is ignored. However, assuming low reverberation times in a
car and ignoring short-time stationary of speech, we propose to estimate
the direct signal PSD (complying with the upper bound of $`N`$) as

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}^{\mathrm{d}}(\hskip-0.5ptk,\hskip-0.5ptl)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\max\big\{\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}(\hskip-0.5ptk,\hskip-0.5ptl)-\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(\hskip-0.5ptk,\hskip-0.5ptl),0\big\}.`$ |  | (24) |

Here, the direct signal PSD estimate
$`\hat{\Phi}_{{Y\hskip-0.5ptY}\!\hskip-0.5pt,m}^{\mathrm{d}}(\hskip-0.5ptk,\hskip-0.5ptl)`$
is lower-limited to avoid negative results due to estimation errors. At
runtime, the right-hand side PSD estimates in
([24](#S4.E24 "In 4.2 Estimation of the Direct Signal PSD ‣ 4 Zone Detection Robust Against ICC Feedback ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
are computed by exponential smoothing of the squared magnitudes of the
according spectra $`{Y}_{m}(k,l)`$ and
$`\hat{Y}_{m}^{\mathrm{fb}}(k,l)`$, respectively (see
[Fig. 3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")).

## 5 Simulation Results

The influence of the proposed direct signal PSD estimation on the
described speech zone detection approach was evaluated in simulations.

Microphone signal simulation: The time-domain microphone signals were
simulated using the signal model described in
[Section 2](#S2 "2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")
at a sampling frequency $`f_{s}\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt24`$ kHz with
a clean female speech source sample. The acoustic impulse responses
$`h_{\mathrm{d},{m}}(n)`$ and $`h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)`$ were measured
in a car (Audi A6) with reverberation time
$`T_{60}\hskip 1.0pt{\approx}\hskip 1.0pt80`$ ms using
$`M\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt4`$ passenger-dedicated microphones as
illustrated in
[Fig. 1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection").
The direct impulse responses $`h_{\mathrm{d},{m}}(n)`$ were measured
with a GRAS 44AA mouth simulator at zone 0 (driver seat), while
$`h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)`$ were measured with
$`L\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt2`$ built-in rear door loudspeakers.
Uncorrelated white noise was added at each microphone
($`\operatorname{SNR}\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt20`$ dB at the reference
microphone). To simulate the ICC system, we only considered a stationary
broadband ICC gain $`\alpha`$ and $`h_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}(n)`$ consisted of
a processing delay
$`\tau_{\mathrm{{ICC}}}\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt15`$ ms and a fixed
gain. The latter gain was adjusted so that the ICC system at
$`\alpha\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$ dB (typical ICC operation gain)
induces the same RMS level at the rear microphones
($`m\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt2,3`$) as at the co-driver microphone
($`m\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt1`$) due to a signal from the driver
seat. For the feedback cancellation filter $`g_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$ in
the ICC system, the measured impulse response $`h_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$
was superimposed by a random, white noise mismatch $`\Delta h_{L,0}(n)`$
(cf. ([9](#S2.E9 "In 2 Signal Model ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))).
It was adjusted so that the simulated ICC system became unstable for
$`\alpha\hskip 1.0pt{>}\hskip 1.0pt4`$ dB, which matches a realistic
system.

Direct signal PSD estimation: The modeled impulse responses
$`\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)`$ and $`\hat{g}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$
which are required for the feedback signal estimation
([Section 3](#S3 "3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
were defined as follows: $`\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,m}(n)`$ was modeled
according to
([14](#S3.E14 "In 3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
(free-field propagation), where the distances $`D_{i,m}`$ between the
ICC loudspeakers and the passenger-dedicated microphones were measured
in the car. Furthermore, the same broadband gain $`\beta_{i,m}`$ was
assumed for all impulse responses (same sensitivity for all loudspeakers
and microphones is assumed). The modeled feedback cancellation filter in
([15](#S3.E15 "In 3 Feedback Signal Estimation ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
was set to
$`\hat{g}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\hat{h}_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$.
We intentionally chose this deviation from the simulated feedback
cancellation filter $`g_{\hskip-0.5ptL,0}(n)`$ to investigate the
robustness against modeling inaccuracies. The feedback signal estimation
and direct signal PSD estimation was implemented in the STFT domain with
Hann-windowed frames of $`N\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt256`$ samples
length (corresponding to $`10.7`$ ms) and $`50\%`$ overlap.

(a) Zone detection rates using unprocessed microphone signal PSDs.

(b) Zone detection rates using the proposed direct signal PSDs.

Fig. 4: Broadband SPR levels for an 8s speech signal at ICC gain
$`\alpha\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$ dB based on the unprocessed
microphone signal PSDs (0s-4s) and on the proposed direct-sound PSD
estimates (4s-8s).

Fig. 5: Zone detection rates of an 8s speech signal in
zone $`\zeta\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$ (driver seat) for different
ICC gains. $`\operatorname{zone\;detection\;rate}(0)`$ (circle markers)
corresponds to the rate of correct detection.

Results and Discussion

[Fig. 5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5 Simulation Results ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")
shows the broadband SPR in
([4.1](#S4.EGx16 "4.1 Energy-Based Speech Zone Detection ‣ 4 Zone Detection Robust Against ICC Feedback ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection"))
of the four passenger-dedicated (= zone-dedicated) microphones for an 8s
speech signal from the driver seat (zone 0) at a typical ICC gain
$`\alpha\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$ dB. The proposed direct signal
PSD estimation was activated after 4s. As can be clearly observed, the
SPR levels without processing (0s-4s) are largely overlapping whereas a
complete separation between the SPR levels of the active zone 0 and the
remaining zones is achieved by the proposed method (4s-8s), even though
the mean SPR levels are shifted by less than $`1`$ dB.

[Fig. 5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5 Simulation Results ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")
shows the zone detection rate of the four speech zones

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\operatorname{zone\;detection\;rate}(\zeta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\#\operatorname{frames\,with}\zeta_{\text{active}}(l)\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt\zeta}{\#\operatorname{total\;frames}}`$ |  | (25) |

for different ICC gains $`\alpha`$, where the same 8s speech signal as
before was used. The $`\operatorname{zone\;detection\;rate}(0)`$ (circle
markers) thus reveals the rate of correct zone detection. The speech
zone detection either directly used the unprocessed microphone signal
PSDs (a) or the estimated direct signal PSDs (b).
[Fig. 5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5 Simulation Results ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")a
shows that the correct zone detection rate based on the microphone
signal PSDs \[[12](#bib.bib12)\] is degraded to less than 50% due to ICC
feedback at a typical ICC gain
$`\alpha\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt0`$ dB. In contrast, the results in
[Fig. 5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5 Simulation Results ‣ Model-Based Estimation of In-Car-Communication Feedbackapplied to Speech Zone Detection")b
indicate a substantial improvement due to the proposed direct signal PSD
estimation, where the ICC-gain can be increased by about $`+6`$ dB to
obtain similar detection rates. Moreover, good speech zone detection
results are obtained until the stability limit of the simulated ICC
system at $`\alpha\hskip 1.0pt{=}\hskip 1.0pt4`$ dB.

## 6 Conclusions

This work described an approach to enhance the robustness of
energy-based speech zone detection against an independently operating,
interfering in-car communication system. The proposed method was
designed in particular to cope with very limited information exchange
between the speech zone detection and the ICC system. Specifically, we
introduced a model-based ICC feedback signal estimation based on a
free-field propagation model between loudspeakers and microphones, which
requires no clean loudspeaker reference signal but only the slowly
time-varying ICC gain. A computational efficient implementation in the
STFT domain was derived consisting of one feed-forward and one recursive
CTF. The resulting feedback signal estimates were used to estimate the
microphone signal PSDs without ICC feedback. Simulations with measured
impulse responses in a car indicated a robustness gain of about $`6`$ dB
against ICC feedback.

While this work considered low-noise scenarios with a simulated ICC
system and speech with frontal head orientation, future work should also
focus noisy environments with a real, more complex ICC system and
different head orientations of a speaker.
````
